name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q01 - Discovery of nuclein and DNA double helix

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: DNA as an acidic substance present in the nucleus was first identified by Friedrich Meischer in \(1869\), who named it 'Nuclein'.

Statement II: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the Double Helix model for DNA in \(1953\) based on X-ray diffraction data produced by Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The discovery of DNA as a nuclear substance and the elucidation of its three-dimensional double-helical structure occurred nearly a century apart.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
Friedrich Meischer first isolated DNA as an acidic substance from the nucleus in \(1869\) and named it 'Nuclein'. In \(1953\), James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the Double Helix model of DNA based on the X-ray diffraction data produced by Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin (along with Erwin Chargaff's base-ratio observations).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q02 - Chemical differences between RNA and DNA

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In RNA, every nucleotide residue has an additional \(-\text{OH}\) group present at the \(2'\)-position in the ribose sugar.

Statement II: In RNA, thymine is found in place of uracil.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA and RNA differ chemically in both their pentose sugar and one of their pyrimidine nitrogenous bases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
Every nucleotide residue in RNA has an additional \(-\text{OH}\) group at the \(2'\)-position of its ribose sugar, which is absent in deoxyribose of DNA. However, in RNA, uracil is found in place of thymine (not thymine in place of uracil).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding the \(2'\text{-OH}\) group in RNA is correct, whereas the claim regarding thymine in RNA is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q03 - DNA packaging in prokaryotes and eukaryotes

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In prokaryotes such as E. coli, positively charged DNA is held with negatively charged proteins in a region termed the nucleoid.

Statement II: In eukaryotes, negatively charged DNA is wrapped around a positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA carries a negative charge due to its phosphate groups and is packaged by interacting with positively charged basic proteins in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
In prokaryotes such as E. coli, DNA is negatively charged (not positively charged) and is held in large loops by positively charged proteins in the nucleoid. In eukaryotes, negatively charged DNA wraps around a positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim about prokaryotic DNA charge is incorrect, whereas the claim about eukaryotic nucleosome formation is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q04 - Outcomes of Griffith transforming principle injections

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In Griffith's experiment, mice infected with the live R strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae died from pneumonia.

Statement II: When Griffith injected heat-killed S strain bacteria alone into mice, the mice died and live S bacteria were recovered.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Griffith's transformation experiments, only live virulent S strain bacteria (with a mucous polysaccharide coat) caused lethal pneumonia in mice.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
Mice injected with live R strain bacteria did not develop pneumonia and lived. Similarly, mice injected with heat-killed S strain bacteria alone also lived. Mice died only when injected with live S strain or a mixture of heat-killed S strain and live R strain bacteria.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q05 - Polarity and continuity at the DNA replication fork

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in one direction, that is, \(5' \to 3'\).

Statement II: At the replication fork, replication is continuous on the template strand with \(3' \to 5'\) polarity and discontinuous on the template strand with \(5' \to 3'\) polarity.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA replication proceeds at a replication fork where the two parental strands have opposite polarities.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
DNA-dependent DNA polymerases can only add nucleotides in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction. Consequently, synthesis on the \(3' \to 5'\) template strand proceeds continuously in the direction of fork opening, whereas synthesis on the \(5' \to 3'\) template strand occurs discontinuously in fragments (which are later joined by DNA ligase).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: Unlike replication where total DNA is duplicated, during transcription only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.

Statement II: If both DNA strands acted as templates simultaneously, they would produce identical RNA molecules that would double the rate of protein synthesis.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transcription copies genetic information from a single strand of a specific DNA segment into RNA.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
During transcription, only one strand of a DNA segment is copied into RNA. If both strands acted as templates simultaneously, they would code for RNA molecules with different (complementary, not identical) sequences, which would code for two different proteins and also base-pair with each other to form double-stranded RNA, preventing translation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim that only one strand of a DNA segment is transcribed is correct, whereas the claim that both strands would yield identical RNA molecules is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q07 - Promoter location and template strand polarity

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In a transcription unit, the promoter is located towards the \(3'\)-end (downstream) of the structural gene with respect to the polarity of the coding strand.

Statement II: The DNA strand that has \(3' \to 5'\) polarity acts as the template strand during transcription.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All positional references in a transcription unit are made with respect to the coding strand (\(5' \to 3'\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
The promoter is located towards the \(5'\)-end (upstream) of the structural gene with respect to the coding strand, while the terminator is at the \(3'\)-end (downstream). Because DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction, the strand with \(3' \to 5'\) polarity acts as the template strand.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim about the promoter being at the \(3'\)-end is incorrect, whereas the claim about the \(3' \to 5'\) strand acting as the template is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q08 - Eukaryotic RNA polymerase I and primary transcripts

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase I transcribes heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), the precursor of mRNA.

Statement II: Eukaryotic primary transcripts lack introns and are immediately functional for translation without splicing.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic transcription involves three nuclear RNA polymerases and extensive post-transcriptional processing of split-gene transcripts.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (\(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\)), whereas RNA polymerase II transcribes hnRNA. Moreover, eukaryotic primary transcripts contain both exons and introns and are non-functional; they must undergo splicing (removal of introns and joining of exons), capping, and tailing before becoming functional mRNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q09 - Frameshift versus triplet insertion or deletion mutations

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases in a structural gene changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion.

Statement II: Insertion or deletion of three or multiples of three bases inserts or deletes one or multiple codons without altering the reading frame from that point onwards.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because the genetic code is read in contiguous triplets without punctuations, the number of bases inserted or deleted determines whether the reading frame shifts.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
Insertion or deletion of one or two bases shifts the triplet reading frame from the mutation site onwards (frameshift insertion or deletion mutations). In contrast, insertion or deletion of three or a multiple of three bases adds or removes one or more complete codons, leaving the downstream reading frame unaltered.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q10 - Repressor synthesis and inducers of lac operon

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In the lac operon, the repressor protein is synthesised constitutively (all the time) from the \(i\) gene.

Statement II: Glucose and galactose act as the primary inducers that inactivate the lac repressor.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The lac operon is under negative regulation by a repressor encoded by the \(i\) gene and is switched on by an inducer.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
The \(i\) gene synthesises the repressor protein constitutively. In the presence of lactose or allolactose (the inducer), the repressor is inactivated, allowing transcription. Glucose or galactose cannot act as inducers for the lac operon.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding constitutive synthesis of the repressor is correct, whereas the claim that glucose and galactose act as inducers is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q11 - Vectors and timeline of Human Genome Project

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: The specialised vectors commonly used for cloning human DNA fragments in the Human Genome Project were BAC (Bioinformatic Artificial Chromosomes) and YAC (Yeast Automated Chromosomes).

Statement II: The Human Genome Project was a \(13\)-year project launched in \(1990\) and completed in \(2003\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project cloned fragmented DNA into bacterial and yeast hosts using specialised artificial chromosome vectors.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
The vectors BAC and YAC stand for Bacterial Artificial Chromosomes and Yeast Artificial Chromosomes, respectively, not Bioinformatic Artificial Chromosomes or Yeast Automated Chromosomes. The project was indeed a \(13\)-year endeavour launched in \(1990\) and completed in \(2003\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding the expansion of BAC and YAC is incorrect, whereas the claim regarding the \(13\)-year timeline is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q12 - Isotope nature and first-generation result in Meselson-Stahl

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In Meselson and Stahl's experiment, \(^{15}\text{N}\) is a radioactive isotope of nitrogen that was detected by autoradiography.

Statement II: After one generation (\(20\text{ minutes}\)) in \(^{14}\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\) medium, the extracted DNA consisted of equal amounts of heavy (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)) and light (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) DNA.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meselson and Stahl proved semiconservative DNA replication in E. coli using density-gradient centrifugation in cesium chloride (\(\text{CsCl}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
\(^{15}\text{N}\) is a heavy, non-radioactive isotope of nitrogen and is separated from \(^{14}\text{N}\) purely based on density in a \(\text{CsCl}\) gradient, not by radioactivity or autoradiography. Furthermore, after one generation (\(20\text{ minutes}\)) in \(^{14}\text{N}\) medium, all extracted DNA had a hybrid or intermediate density (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)), not a mixture of heavy and light DNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q13 - Stability and roles of DNA versus RNA

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: RNA mutates at a faster rate than DNA because the \(2'\text{-OH}\) group present at every nucleotide in RNA is reactive and makes RNA labile and easily degradable.

Statement II: DNA, being chemically more stable, is preferred for storage of genetic information, whereas RNA is better for the transmission of genetic information.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Structural and chemical differences between DNA and RNA determine their relative stability and biological roles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
The \(2'\text{-OH}\) group in RNA is reactive and makes RNA labile and easily degradable, so RNA mutates and evolves faster than DNA. Because DNA is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable (also aided by thymine and double-stranded repair), DNA is preferred for storing genetic information, while RNA (which can directly code for protein synthesis) is better for transmitting genetic information.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q14 - Evolutionary significance of introns and bacterial mRNA

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: The presence of introns in eukaryotic genes is reminiscent of antiquity, and the process of splicing represents the dominance of the RNA-world.

Statement II: In bacteria, transcription and translation cannot be coupled because bacterial mRNA must undergo capping and tailing before translation.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Split-gene arrangements and RNA processing distinguish eukaryotic gene expression from prokaryotic gene expression.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
Split-gene arrangements are an ancient feature of the genome: the presence of introns is reminiscent of antiquity, and splicing reflects the dominance of the RNA-world. However, in bacteria, mRNA does not require any processing (no capping, tailing, or splicing) and there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus, so transcription and translation CAN be coupled.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding introns and splicing is correct, whereas the claim that bacterial transcription and translation cannot be coupled is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q15 - Repetitive sequences and base similarity in human genome

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: In the human genome, repeated sequences make up less than \(2\%\) of the genome and directly code for essential enzymes.

Statement II: Almost all (\(99.9\%\)) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all people.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Salient observations from the Human Genome Project highlight the proportion of coding DNA, repetitive DNA, and inter-individual similarity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
Less than \(2\%\) of the human genome codes for proteins, whereas repeated sequences make up a very large portion of the human genome and are thought to have no direct coding functions. On the other hand, almost all (\(99.9\%\)) nucleotide bases are indeed identical across all humans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim about repeated sequences is incorrect, whereas the claim about \(99.9\%\) nucleotide similarity among humans is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_STMT2_Q16 - VNTR banding in twins and Southern blotting transfer

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and select the correct option:

Statement I: DNA fingerprinting banding patterns differ between monozygotic (identical) twins.

Statement II: In Southern blot hybridisation, VNTR belongs to micro-satellites, and DNA fragments are transferred from a nitrocellulose membrane onto an agarose gel.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA fingerprinting relies on polymorphism in mini-satellite VNTR sequences separated by gel electrophoresis and blotted onto synthetic membranes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Both Propositions
DNA fingerprinting patterns differ from individual to individual in a population EXCEPT in the case of monozygotic (identical) twins, who share the same DNA fingerprint. Additionally, VNTR belongs to the mini-satellite class of satellite DNA (not micro-satellite), and separated DNA fragments are transferred from the electrophoresis gel onto synthetic membranes such as nitrocellulose or nylon (not the reverse).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both propositions are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
